claims.text: A page exists at /docs/support/provider-support-policy/ (the Pulumi docs 'Provider support policy' page) that the support index links to.
The Pulumi 'Provider support policy' docs page describes how long Pulumi maintains each provider major version.
The Pulumi 'Provider support policy' docs page describes which providers get long-term security updates (i.e., some Pulumi providers receive long-term security updates).

Pulumi does not automatically roll back changes made during an update if an error or failure occurs; it completes any pending operations currently in progress, then exits and reports the error or failure.
To perform a manual rollback after a failed deployment, revert the code and configuration changes of the failed deployment and run `pulumi up` to return infrastructure to its previous state.

Pulumi does not automatically query the cloud provider's live state before running `pulumi up` or `pulumi preview`; it compares the desired state declared in the program against the last recorded state to determine changes.

Not refreshing state automatically before every update is an intentional Pulumi design decision, because refreshing requires a round-trip to the cloud provider for every resource in a stack, adding significant latency for large stacks.
Running `pulumi refresh` synchronizes Pulumi's recorded state with the actual state of the cloud resources.
`pulumi up --refresh` refreshes state and applies the desired state in a single step.
Pulumi Cloud provides built-in drift detection for automated drift detection and remediation on a schedule (Pulumi Deployments drift detection).
The page /docs/deployments/concepts/drift/ exists and documents Pulumi Cloud drift detection.
The 'Refreshing state' section at /docs/iac/concepts/state-and-backends/#refreshing-state exists and explains refresh behavior in detail.

In Pulumi, a resource's logical name is part of the auto-assigned resource URN, while the physical name is how the resource is known to the cloud provider; the logical name only needs to be unique within a stack, whereas the physical name typically needs to be unique within a certain scope (sometimes globally).

Pulumi automatically creates each resource's physical name by combining the logical name with a random suffix appended afterwards, so that many logical resources and stacks can be stood up side-by-side without conflict.
Pulumi auto-naming lets Pulumi replace resources with less downtime by creating the replacement before deleting the old resource.
An auto-named resource's physical name typically looks like `my-bucket-d7c2fa0` rather than `my-bucket` (a random hex suffix).
Auto-naming can be disabled on a per-resource basis, which yields precise physical names without random suffixes but loses the benefits of auto-naming.
The section /docs/iac/concepts/resources/names/#autonaming exists and documents auto-naming.
Project or stack configuration can be used to customize or disable auto-naming globally, per provider, or per resource type.
The section /docs/iac/concepts/resources/names/#autonaming-configuration ('Auto-naming Configuration') exists.
During a Pulumi update, secrets are decrypted in memory and visible to the Pulumi program; persisting them outside Pulumi securely is the user's responsibility.
Pulumi provides primitives to store secrets securely in the CLI, the state file, and Pulumi Cloud.
Passing `--secret` to `pulumi config set` causes the configuration value to be encrypted so it can be safely persisted in `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml`.
Pulumi Cloud manages a unique encryption key for every stack, used to encrypt secrets for that stack, and this is configurable to use a custom secrets provider.
Because a different encryption key is used per stack, encrypting the same value in two different stacks produces different encrypted strings in the `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml` files.
An encrypted config value cannot be copied from one stack config file to another using a text editor; `pulumi config set` must be used instead.
When running a preview, update, or destroy, Pulumi decrypts secret config data; it is plain text during execution and any part of the Pulumi program can access it through the Pulumi config object.
Pulumi does not use the Terraform engine in any way.
Some Pulumi providers use the open-source Terraform schemas to determine available resources and parameters and to determine return and response attributes.
Pulumi native providers are mapped directly to cloud provider APIs and do not use Terraform schemas.
The blog post at /blog/pulumiup-native-providers/ exists and covers Pulumi native providers.
Pulumi is a declarative tool that uses imperative languages to define the end state; the language is used for authoring the program and not for talking to the cloud provider API.
Pulumi uses strongly typed languages that support IntelliSense and the Language Server Protocol, so users rarely need to leave their IDE when defining Pulumi programs.
Experimental Pulumi features are always opt-in, enabled explicitly with a flag, command, or environment variable such as `PULUMI_EXPERIMENTAL=true`.
Pulumi experimental features are not necessarily supported and can change or be removed at any time without a deprecation cycle.
When an experimental feature proves valuable, Pulumi invests in stabilizing it and promoting it to general availability.
Pulumi's policy is to focus on actively supporting the latest released major version of the providers Pulumi maintains.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi also ships security updates for the previous major version for up to a year, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
The provider support policy page (/docs/support/provider-support-policy/) lists the covered providers and what a long-term support release contains.
Older major versions of Pulumi-maintained providers (beyond the latest major, and beyond any security-update window for the previous major) receive no patches at all.
The Pulumi Registry (/registry/) lists the current version for all providers maintained by Pulumi.
Updating to the latest provider version gives access to the most recent features, bug fixes, and security enhancements.
Major provider versions typically include significant changes such as deprecations, new resources and new functionality, which may require additional migration steps.
Pulumi recommends treating the release of a provider major version as a signal to begin planning a provider version update.
Pulumi recommends updating to the latest minor version on the current major provider version at least quarterly and minimally reviewing provider release notes.
Provider minor versions typically include new resources and features, performance improvements, and bug fixes without introducing breaking changes.
The release notes for each provider release summarize the new capabilities or fixes.
In npm, the tilde operator (e.g., `~1.2.3`) allows patch updates on the current minor version.
Pulumi recommends always allowing patch updates on the current minor provider version.
Provider patch versions are primarily for bug fixes and security updates and are designed to be fully backward compatible.
Pulumi recommends never being two major provider versions behind, since jumping a major version is inadvisable due to the number of potential breaking changes.

Each major version of a Pulumi provider includes migration logic to smooth the upgrade from the immediately previous major version, but these migrations do not always work across multiple major versions.
The Provider support policy page at /docs/support/provider-support-policy/ exists.
The pages /docs/support/faq/secrets-config/ (Pulumi ESC FAQ), /docs/support/faq/pulumi-cloud/ (Pulumi Cloud FAQ), and /docs/support/faq/policies/ (Pulumi Policies FAQ) exist.
Pulumi actively maintains the latest released major version of every provider it publishes.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi ships security updates for the previous major version for up to 12 months, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
The providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions are: AWS, Azure Classic, Azure Native, Azure AD, Command, Docker Build, GCP, Kubernetes, TLS, and Vault.
The Pulumi AWS provider is covered by Pulumi's long-term support policy and its registry page is at /registry/packages/aws/.
Registry package pages exist at /registry/packages/ for aws, azure, azure-native, azuread, command, docker-build, gcp, kubernetes, tls, and vault.
The LTS branch of a covered Pulumi provider ships High/Critical CVE security patches, including fixes for CVEs affecting the provider's code or its direct dependencies.
The LTS branch of a covered Pulumi provider ships fixes for broken internal infrastructure on the LTS branch needed to ship the security patches.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain new upstream API versions.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain new resources or new resource properties.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain performance improvements.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain non-security bug fixes.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain compatibility with newer versions of language runtimes.
Pulumi LTS provider releases remain compatible with the version of the Pulumi engine they were frozen at, unless security fixes require otherwise.
Under Pulumi's provider support policy, exactly one long-term support major version exists per covered provider at any time.
Under Pulumi's provider support policy, when major version N+1 of a covered provider ships, it becomes the new N and the old N becomes the new LTS major.
Under Pulumi's provider support policy, the old long-term support major version reaches end of life on the same day N+1 ships, regardless of how much of its 12-month window remained.
Within the long-term support major version of a covered Pulumi provider, only the latest minor version receives patches and earlier minor versions are frozen.
Pulumi provider LTS releases are available through the same standard package registries as current-major releases, but are tagged differently.
Customers pinning a Pulumi provider to a specific major version is the recommended practice, and they automatically receive patch releases as they ship.
At any time, exactly one major version of a covered Pulumi provider is the LTS version, and older majors receive no patches.
N is the latest released major version: if v3 is the newest release, then v3 is N, v2 is N−1 (LTS), and v1 and earlier are end of life.

The current major version (N) of a Pulumi provider is supported until N+1 ships and receives new features, new resources, bug fixes, security patches, dependency upgrades, and new upstream API versions.

The long-term support version (N−1) of a covered Pulumi provider is supported for up to 12 months from N's release, or until N+1 ships, and receives security updates in the provider's code or its direct dependencies.
End-of-life Pulumi provider versions (N−2 and older) are not supported and will not receive updates.

The Pulumi support FAQ at /docs/support/faq/infrastructure/ contains a section 'What are the best practices for maintaining provider versions' (anchor #what-are-the-best-practices-for-maintaining-provider-versions).
Pages exist at /registry/ (Pulumi Registry) and /docs/support/getting-support/ (Getting support).
